name: Venlafaxine
className: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) antidepressant

src.q: Each prolonged-release capsule contains 84.85 mg of venlafaxine hydrochloride, equivalent to 75 mg of venlafaxine free base.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Major depressive episodes (treatment and prevention of recurrence); generalised anxiety disorder; social anxiety disorder; panic disorder with or without agoraphobia.

src.q: Treatment of major depressive episodes. For prevention of recurrence of major depressive episodes. Treatment of generalised anxiety disorder.
Treatment of social anxiety disorder. Treatment of panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia.

items.t: Not recommended for children and adolescents under 18 years.

src.q: Venlafaxine is not recommended for use in children and adolescents.

items.t: Prescribe the smallest quantity consistent with good patient management, to reduce overdose risk (fatal overdoses reported, mainly with alcohol or other medicines).

src.q: Prescriptions for venlafaxine should be written for the smallest quantity consistent with good patient management, in order to reduce the risk of overdose
Overdose with venlafaxine has been reported predominantly in combination with alcohol and/or other medicinal products, including cases with fatal outcome

items.t: Start 75 mg once daily. If no response, increase up to a maximum of 375 mg/day, at intervals of 2 weeks or more (not less than 4 days if clinically warranted). Increase only after clinical evaluation; keep the lowest effective dose. Continue for at least 6 months after remission.

src.q: The recommended starting dose for prolonged-release venlafaxine is 75 mg given once daily.
may benefit from dose increases up to a maximum dose of 375 mg/day
If clinically warranted due to symptom severity, dose increases can be made at more frequent intervals, but not less than 4 days.
Antidepressive medicinal products should continue for at least six months following remission.

items.t: Start 75 mg once daily. If no response, increase up to a maximum of 225 mg/day, at intervals of 2 weeks or more.

src.q: Generalised anxiety disorder The recommended starting dose for prolonged-release venlafaxine is 75 mg given once daily.
may benefit from dose increases up to a maximum dose of 225 mg/day

items.t: 75 mg once daily. No evidence that higher doses add benefit, but up to a maximum of 225 mg/day may be considered in non-responders (intervals of 2 weeks or more).

src.q: The recommended dose for prolonged-release venlafaxine is 75 mg given once daily. There is no evidence that higher doses confer any additional benefit.
increases up to a maximum dose of 225 mg/day may be considered

items.t: 37.5 mg/day for 7 days, then 75 mg/day. If no response, increase up to a maximum of 225 mg/day (intervals of 2 weeks or more).

src.q: It is recommended that a dose of 37.5 mg/day of prolonged-release venlafaxine be used for 7 days. Dosage should then be increased to 75 mg/day.

items.t: Elderly: no dose change for age alone, but use caution (possible renal impairment, changed sensitivity); use the lowest effective dose and monitor carefully when increasing.

src.q: No specific dose adjustments of venlafaxine are considered necessary based on patient age alone. However, caution should be exercised in treating the elderly
patients should be carefully monitored when an increase in the dose is required

items.t: Switching from immediate-release tablets: use the nearest equivalent daily dose (e.g. 37.5 mg twice daily to 75 mg once daily).

src.q: venlafaxine immediate-release tablets 37.5 mg twice daily may be switched to venlafaxine prolonged-release capsules 75 mg once daily.

items.t: Stopping: avoid abrupt withdrawal. Reduce gradually over at least 1 to 2 weeks; some patients need months or longer. If intolerable symptoms, go back to the previous dose and taper more slowly.

src.q: When stopping treatment with venlafaxine, the dose should be gradually reduced over a period of at least one to two weeks in order to reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions
In some patients, discontinuation may need to occur very gradually over periods of months or longer.

items.t: Not recommended under 18 years. Trials in major depressive disorder did not show efficacy; safety and efficacy for other indications not established. If used on clinical need, monitor carefully for suicidal symptoms.

src.q: Controlled clinical studies in children and adolescents with major depressive disorder failed to demonstrate efficacy
If, based on clinical need, a decision to treat is nevertheless taken, the patient should be carefully monitored for the appearance of suicidal symptoms.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to venlafaxine or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Irreversible MAOIs: contraindicated (serotonin syndrome). Do not start venlafaxine within 14 days of stopping an irreversible MAOI; stop venlafaxine at least 7 days before starting one.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) is contraindicated due to the risk of serotonin syndrome
Venlafaxine must not be initiated for at least 14 days after discontinuation of treatment with an irreversible MAOI.
Venlafaxine must be discontinued for at least 7 days before starting treatment with an irreversible MAOI

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (can resemble NMS), especially with other serotonergic drugs, MAOIs, antipsychotics or other dopamine antagonists. If combined use is needed, observe carefully at start and after dose increases. Tryptophan supplements: not recommended.

src.q: As with other serotonergic agents, serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition may occur with venlafaxine treatment
careful observation of the patient is advised, particularly during treatment initiation and dose increases
The concomitant use of venlafaxine with serotonin precursors (such as tryptophan supplements) is not recommended.

items.t: Blood pressure: dose-related rises are common; severe rises needing urgent treatment reported. Screen for and control hypertension before starting; review BP periodically and after dose increases. Caution if raised BP or heart rate could harm (e.g. impaired cardiac function).

src.q: Dose-related increases in blood pressure have been commonly reported with venlafaxine.
All patients should be carefully screened for high blood pressure and pre-existing hypertension should be controlled before initation of treatment.
Blood pressure should be reviewed periodically, after initiation of treatment and after dose increases.
Caution should be exercised in patients whose underlying conditions might be compromised by increases in blood pressure, e.g., those with impaired cardiac function.

items.t: Heart disease and arrhythmia: not studied after recent myocardial infarction or in unstable heart disease (use with caution). QTc prolongation, torsade de pointes and fatal arrhythmias reported; weigh risks and benefits if at high risk of arrhythmia or QTc prolongation.

src.q: Venlafaxine has not been evaluated in patients with a recent history of myocardial infarction or unstable heart disease. Therefore, it should be used with caution in these patients.
The balance of risks and benefits should be considered before prescribing venlafaxine to patients at high risk of serious cardiac arrhythmia or QTc prolongation

items.t: Seizures: introduce with caution if history of convulsions; stop if seizures develop.

src.q: venlafaxine should be introduced with caution in patients with a history of convulsions
Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures.

items.t: Hyponatraemia / SIADH: higher risk in elderly, volume-depleted or dehydrated patients and those taking diuretics.

src.q: Cases of hyponatraemia and/or the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH) secretion may occur with venlafaxine.
Elderly patients, patients taking diuretics, and patients who are otherwise volume-depleted may be at greater risk for this event.

items.t: Bleeding (bruising to GI and life-threatening haemorrhage): use cautiously if predisposed to bleeding, including with anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors. May increase postpartum haemorrhage.

src.q: venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients predisposed to bleeding, including patients on anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors.
SSRIs/SNRIs, including venlafaxine, may increase the risk of postpartum haemorrhage

items.t: Mydriasis: closely monitor patients with raised intraocular pressure or at risk of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

src.q: It is recommended that patients with raised intraocular pressure or patients at risk for acute narrow-angle glaucoma (angle-closure glaucoma) be closely monitored.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts and clinical worsening: monitor closely until improvement, especially early in treatment and after dose changes. Higher risk of suicidal behaviour under 25 years.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored until such improvement occurs
increased risk of suicidal behaviour with antidepressants compared to placebo in patients less than 25 years old

items.t: Mania/hypomania: use cautiously with a history or family history of bipolar disorder. Aggression: use cautiously with a history of aggression.

src.q: venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients with a history or family history of bipolar disorder.
venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients with a history of aggression.

items.t: Diabetes: glycaemic control may change; insulin and/or oral antidiabetic doses may need adjusting.

src.q: In patients with diabetes, treatment with an SSRI or venlafaxine may alter glycaemic control. Insulin and/or oral antidiabetic dosage may need to be adjusted.

items.t: Serum cholesterol may rise: consider measuring it during long-term treatment.

src.q: Measurement of serum cholesterol levels should be considered during long-term treatment.

items.t: Sexual dysfunction may occur and can continue after stopping. Akathisia may occur in the first weeks; increasing the dose may be harmful.

src.q: There have been reports of long-lasting sexual dysfunction where the symptoms have continued despite discontinuation of SNRIs
In patients who develop these symptoms, increasing the dose may be detrimental.

items.t: Weight-loss agents (e.g. phentermine): co-administration not recommended.

src.q: Co-administration of venlafaxine and weight loss agents is not recommended.

items.t: False-positive urine immunoassay screens for phencyclidine and amphetamine; confirm with GC/MS.

src.q: False-positive urine immunoassay screening tests for phencyclidine (PCP) and amphetamine have been reported in patients taking venlafaxine.

items.t: Irreversible non-selective MAOIs: contraindicated. Moclobemide: not recommended. Linezolid: should not be given.

src.q: Venlafaxine must not be used in combination with irreversible non-selective MAOIs.
the combination of venlafaxine with a reversible and selective MAOI, such as moclobemide, is not recommended
The antibiotic linezolid is a weak reversible and non-selective MAOI and should not be given to patients treated with venlafaxine

items.t: Serotonergic drugs (triptans, SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, lithium, St John's wort, opioids such as tramadol and dextromethorphan) and antipsychotics/dopamine antagonists: serotonin syndrome risk; observe carefully, especially at start and after dose increases.

src.q: including triptans, SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, amphetamines, lithium, sibutramine
opioids [e.g., buprenorphine, fentanyl and its analogues, tramadol, dextromethorphan, tapentadol, pethidine, methadone and pentazocine]
or with antipsychotics or other dopamine antagonists
careful observation of the patient is advised, particularly during treatment initiation and dose increases

items.t: QT-prolonging medicines (class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics, some macrolides such as erythromycin, some antihistamines, some quinolones such as moxifloxacin): avoid co-administration.

src.q: Co-administration of such medicinal products should be avoided
some macrolides (e.g., erythromycin) some antihistamines some quinolone antibiotics (e.g., moxifloxacin)

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, ritonavir): may raise venlafaxine levels; caution.

src.q: Concomitant use of CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., atazanavir, clarithromycin, indinavir, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole,
Therefore, caution is advised if a patient's therapy includes a CYP3A4 inhibitor and venlafaxine concomitantly.

items.t: Other CNS-active drugs: caution. Alcohol: advise patients not to drink.

src.q: caution is advised when venlafaxine is taken in combination with other CNS-active substances
Patients should be advised not to use alcohol

items.t: Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors: higher bleeding risk; use cautiously.

src.q: venlafaxine should be used cautiously in patients predisposed to bleeding, including patients on anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors.

items.t: Metoprolol (levels up 30 to 40%) and imipramine: caution. Haloperidol levels rise (clinical significance unknown).

src.q: Caution should be exercised with co-administration of venlafaxine and metoprolol.
Caution should be exercised with co-administration of venlafaxine and imipramine.

items.t: GFR 30 to 70 mL/min: no dose change needed, but caution. Severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min) or haemodialysis: reduce dose by 50%; individualise.

src.q: Although no change in dosage is necessary for patients with glomerular filtration rate (GFR) between 30-70 ml/minute, caution is advised.
For patients that require haemodialysis and in patients with severe renal impairment (GFR < 30 ml/min), the dose should be reduced by 50%.

items.t: Mild or moderate hepatic impairment: consider a 50% dose reduction (individualise). Severe: limited data; caution, consider reducing by more than 50%, weigh benefit against risk.

src.q: In patients with mild and moderate hepatic impairment, in general a 50% dose reduction should be considered.
Caution is advised, and a dose reduction by more than 50% should be considered.

items.t: SmPC: no adequate human data; use only if the expected benefit outweighs any possible risk.

src.q: Venlafaxine must only be administered to pregnant women if the expected benefits outweigh any possible risk.

items.t: Use until or shortly before birth: neonatal withdrawal/serotonergic symptoms; some newborns needed tube-feeding, respiratory support or long hospital stay. PPHN risk cannot be ruled out.

src.q: Some newborns exposed to venlafaxine late in the third trimester have developed complications requiring tube-feeding, respiratory support or prolonged hospitalisation.
this potential risk cannot be ruled out with venlafaxine

items.t: Use in the month before delivery: small increased risk (less than 2-fold) of postpartum haemorrhage. MHRA: weigh this against the individual bleeding/thrombotic risk and the benefits of treatment.

src.q: Observational data indicate an increased risk (less than 2-fold) of postpartum haemorrhage following SSRIs/SNRIs exposure within the month prior to birth
consider the findings of the review in the context of individual patient risk factors for bleeding or thrombotic events

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no good evidence of effects on the baby's development. Late-pregnancy use usually means birth in hospital (neonatal checks).

src.q: Venlafaxine can be used in pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
There is no good evidence that venlafaxine affects your baby's development.

items.t: SmPC: venlafaxine and its active metabolite pass into milk; infant crying, irritability and abnormal sleep reported. Decide whether to continue breastfeeding or treatment, weighing benefits.

src.q: Venlafaxine and its active metabolite, O-desmethylvenlafaxine, are excreted in breast milk.
A risk to the suckling child cannot be excluded.

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution and infant monitoring, but SSRIs or tricyclics are preferred. Monitor the infant for irritability, agitation, colic, drowsiness, GI symptoms, poor feeding and weight gain. No need to switch if used successfully in pregnancy (full-term healthy infant).

src.q: Venlafaxine can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but SSRIs or TCAs are preferred.
Monitor infants for irritability, agitation, colic, drowsiness, gastrointestinal symptoms, poor feeding or not waking to feed and appropriate weight gain.
If duloxetine, mirtazapine, trazodone or venlafaxine have been used successfully during pregnancy, there is no need to switch to a preferred choice in breastfeeding

items.t: Reduced fertility seen in rats exposed to the active metabolite; human relevance unknown. Unintended pregnancies reported with oral contraceptives, with no clear evidence of an interaction (not studied).

src.q: Reduced fertility was observed in a study in which both male and female rats were exposed to O-desmethylvenlafaxine.
There is no clear evidence these pregnancies were a result of drug interaction with venlafaxine.

items.t: Very common: nausea, dry mouth, headache, sweating (including night sweats).

src.q: Adverse reactions reported as very common (>1/10) in clinical studies were nausea, dry mouth, headache and sweating (including night sweats).

items.t: Dose-related blood pressure increases are common. Withdrawal symptoms are common on stopping (dizziness, sensory disturbances, sleep disturbance, agitation, nausea, tremor, headache).

src.q: Dose-related increases in blood pressure have been commonly reported with venlafaxine.
Withdrawal symptoms, when treatment is discontinued, are common, particularly if discontinuation is abrupt

items.t: Serotonin syndrome / NMS-like reactions: potentially life-threatening.

src.q: As with other serotonergic agents, serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition may occur with venlafaxine treatment

items.t: Severely raised blood pressure needing immediate treatment.

src.q: In some cases, severely elevated blood pressure requiring immediate treatment has been reported in postmarketing experience.

items.t: QTc prolongation, torsade de pointes, ventricular tachycardia, fatal arrhythmias (especially in overdose or with risk factors).

src.q: cases of QTc prolongation, Torsade de Pointes (TdP), ventricular tachycardia, and fatal cardiac arrhythmias have been reported with the use of venlafaxine

items.t: Seizures: stop treatment.

src.q: Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour and aggression, including on dose reduction or stopping: monitor closely.

src.q: patients should be closely monitored when the dose is reduced or during discontinuation

items.t: Overdose may carry a higher risk of fatal outcome than SSRIs (lower than tricyclics).

src.q: Published retrospective studies report that venlafaxine overdosage may be associated with an increased risk of fatal outcomes compared to that observed with SSRI antidepressant products

items.t: Screen for high blood pressure and control hypertension before starting. Discuss the risk of suicidal thoughts and of sexual dysfunction when starting or changing dose (MHRA 2026).

src.q: All patients should be carefully screened for high blood pressure and pre-existing hypertension should be controlled before initation of treatment.
discuss with patients when starting or changing the dose of an antidepressant or at their next review, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours

items.t: Blood pressure periodically and after each dose increase. Close monitoring for clinical worsening and suicidality early on, after dose changes and when stopping. Monitor regularly after starting (MHRA). Consider serum cholesterol in long-term use.

src.q: Blood pressure should be reviewed periodically, after initiation of treatment and after dose increases.
monitor your patients regularly after starting treatment with an antidepressant
Measurement of serum cholesterol levels should be considered during long-term treatment.

items.t: Stop if seizures develop. Taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures.
It is therefore advised that venlafaxine should be gradually tapered when discontinuing treatment over a period of several weeks or months, according to the patient's needs

items.t: Take with food at about the same time each day. Swallow whole with fluid; do not divide, crush, chew or dissolve. Empty capsule spheroids may be seen in faeces.

src.q: It is recommended that venlafaxine prolonged-release capsules be taken with food, at approximately the same time each day.
Capsules must be swallowed whole with fluid and not divided, crushed, chewed, or dissolved.
The insoluble portion of these spheroids is eliminated and may be seen in faeces.

items.t: Do not drink alcohol. Do not stop suddenly: withdrawal symptoms can occur, even after a missed dose.

src.q: Patients should be advised not to use alcohol
there have been very rare reports of such symptoms in patients who have inadvertently missed a dose

items.t: Seek urgent medical help for new or worsening suicidal thoughts, especially when starting or changing dose. Sexual dysfunction may continue after stopping.

src.q: if you have new or worsening suicidal thoughts, particularly when starting or changing dose of antidepressants, seek urgent medical attention
there is the potential for you to experience sexual dysfunction with some antidepressants, which may continue even after you stop the medicine

items.t: Take care with driving or machinery. Dry mouth is common: keep good dental hygiene.

src.q: any patient receiving venlafaxine should be cautioned about their ability to drive or operate hazardous machinery
